structure.title: Books I–II · Government in Hell
structure.text: The fallen angels gather after a ruinous defeat. Milton gives them architecture, competing policies and eloquent speakers. It takes some listening to tell when the great debate begins to ratify an adventure its leader already wants.

structure.title: Books III–IV · Heaven looks down, Satan looks in
structure.text: From Heaven the future of humankind is already visible. From the edge of Eden Satan gets his first sight of two people happy together. His response to their pleasure supplies a motive no military speech could fully explain.

structure.title: Books V–VIII · A guest in the garden
structure.text: Raphael visits for a meal and a long conversation. The war in Heaven, creation and Adam's own memories enter through questions at the table. Adam and Eve have a household to run while an angel explains the magnitude of their danger.

structure.title: Books IX–XII · One working day and its aftermath
structure.text: A discussion about dividing the gardening work opens a gap in the couple's routine. Afterwards they must learn how blame, shame and forgiveness work between two people. The poem finally opens their story onto generations neither will meet.

people.name: Satan
people.text: He adapts quickly to an audience. Among soldiers he offers glory, alone he can entertain despair, and in Eden he finds an attentive listener who knows little of either emotion.

people.name: Adam and Eve
people.text: They plan a day's labour, receive a guest and tell stories about meeting each other. Their disagreements carry weight because the poem has first given them habits and an intelligible pleasure in one another's company.

context.title: Foreknowledge and freedom
context.text: In Milton's Heaven God knows the outcome in advance and holds that the choice remains free. Scenes on earth unfold slowly enough for the reader to hear arguments and alternatives as they occur to people who do not know the future.

notice.text: When does Satan borrow a noble word?
notice.why: Liberty, service and honour sound very different in the mouth of a rebel who expects his own followers to obey him. His audience changes more often than his appetite for command.
What should one serve an angel? The preparations give her choices, knowledge and practical skill. They also make Eden a place where the loss of a particular way of living can be felt.

opening: Satan has lost a war against God and immediately begins explaining why defeat need not count as defeat. His speeches make rebellion sound magnificent, even as revenge becomes his governing purpose. Meanwhile Adam and Eve inhabit a world they have not yet learned to distrust. Milton gives the catastrophe of the Fall the scale of an epic and the intimacy of a relationship: persuasion, pride, tenderness, and the terrible possibility of choosing something because the person you love has already chosen it.
